title: Progress: is this approach effective, and why?
blurb: Judge tolerances, reporting frequency, time-driven and event-driven controls, forecasting and exception handling in a scenario, and give the reason that fits.
question: At Wenmoor Community Health, the project manager is new to PRINCE2 and the team has never worked together. The board asks for weekly rather than monthly highlight reports during the pilot. How well does this apply the progress practice, and why?

teach.body: When judging progress control, check four things. Are tolerances set by the right level, for the right aspects? Is reporting proportionate: more frequent for an inexperienced team, lighter for an experienced one, in a format that suits the audience? Are both time-driven reporting and event-driven decisions in place? And is escalation triggered by a forecast breach at the right level, with work package deviations handled by the project manager and no exception report while the stage stays within tolerance?

rows.label: Examples
values: Stage end, PID complete, exception report

teach.caption: Every stage needs both: monitoring is time-based, decision-making is event-based (11.2.2).

steps.label: Board decides
steps.sub: For example, ask for an exception plan (DP)

teach.caption: 11.3.1. A project tolerance breach is decided by the business layer, not the board.

teach.h: Escalate on the forecast, not the actual
teach.caption: An exception is a FORECAST breach: escalate at report 5, when the forecast crosses tolerance, not when the stage actually ends late.

In a work package description?
rows: Yes: agreed between PM and team manager
No: not agreed for a work package
No: from acceptance criteria and product specifications
No: a WP description carries only time, cost and scope
teach.caption: The sample rationales confirm benefits and quality tolerances are not agreed in a work package description.

teach.body: Reporting frequency should match the control needed: for an inexperienced team the PM or board may report more often until confidence grows; an experienced team can report less often. Progress can only be controlled at the level of detail in the plans, and reviews should look forward with forecasts, not just record what happened. Data and systems help: stored past performance supports forecasting and automation saves manual consolidation. But data does not set tolerances; management levels do.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Wenmoor single point of access
teach.body: Wenmoor's executive team, the business layer, sets project tolerances of plus or minus 10% cost and one month on the end of roll-out. The board sets tighter pilot stage tolerances. Because project manager Ellie Chandran is new to PRINCE2 and the part-time team is new, the board asks for weekly highlight reports, given as a short online call at lunchtime. A four-day slip in training materials stays within stage tolerance, so Ellie takes corrective action. When the supplier forecasts a three-week configuration delay, beyond stage tolerance, she raises an exception report.

items: Find the tolerance and the level: work package, stage or project?
Is the breach forecast, and does it cross that level's tolerance? Then escalate one level up.
Is reporting proportionate to experience, risk and audience?
Pick the reason that explains this case, not a general truth about progress.

teach.text: Traps: (1) an exception is a FORECAST breach, so waiting for the actual overrun is poor practice; (2) within stage tolerance there is no exception report; (3) work package exceptions are handled by the PM, stage exceptions by the board, project exceptions by the business layer; (4) highlight reports are time-driven, while stage ends and exception reports are event-driven.

items: Reporting frequency fits the team: more often for inexperienced teams.
Every stage needs time-driven reporting and event-driven decisions.
Escalate as soon as a breach is forecast, to the level that set the tolerance.
Work package descriptions carry time, cost and scope tolerances, not benefits or quality.
Data supports forecasting; it does not set tolerances.

summary: You can now judge whether tolerances, reporting frequency and format, time-driven and event-driven controls, forecasting and escalation are applied well in a scenario. You can also explain the verdict with the reason that fits the situation rather than a general truth.

A.q: Wenmoor Community Health's single point of access project is about to start its Eastfield pilot. Project manager Ellie Chandran is new to PRINCE2, and most of the team have never worked together. The board asks for weekly highlight reports during the pilot instead of monthly ones. How well does this apply the progress practice, and why?
options: Well, because highlight reports are event-driven
Well, because inexperience calls for closer control
Poorly, because the board should manage by exception
Poorly, because frequency is fixed in the PID
A.why: Reporting frequency should reflect the control needed; for an inexperienced team the PM or board may increase frequency until confidence grows (11.2.4).

whyNot.0: Highlight reports are time-driven, produced at intervals set by the board.
whyNot.2: The board does manage by exception, but that does not stop it choosing a suitable reporting frequency.
whyNot.3: Frequency is agreed and can be adjusted as the level of control needed changes.

A.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in its factory trials stage, which has a time tolerance of two weeks. The Dutch line supplier's project engineer reports that commissioning will finish late, and project manager Nadia Osei now forecasts that the stage will end three weeks late. What should she do?
options: Ask the team to work faster and report at stage end
Wait until the stage actually overruns, then report
Ask the business layer for more project tolerance
Raise an exception report to the project board
A.why: When stage tolerance is forecast to be exceeded, the PM escalates to the board with an exception report in controlling a stage (11.2.6, 11.3.1).

whyNot.0: Corrective action is for deviations within tolerance; a forecast stage breach must be escalated now.
whyNot.1: An exception is a forecast breach, so waiting for the actual overrun delays the board's decision.
whyNot.2: Stage tolerance belongs to the board; the PM escalates to the board, not the business layer.

A.q: Calderbrook's Permits Online project is in the private beta stage, which has a time tolerance of two weeks. A work package is forecast to finish four days late, but the stage is still forecast to finish within its tolerance. What should project manager Hannah Okoro do?
options: Take corrective action within the stage
Raise an exception report to the board
Ask the board for an exception plan
Escalate it to the business layer as an issue
A.why: If the PM can resolve a deviation within stage tolerance, no exception report is needed; corrective action is taken in controlling a stage (11.2.6, 16.4.6).

whyNot.1: Exception reports are for a forecast breach of stage or project tolerance.
whyNot.2: Exception plans are requested by the board after an exception report, which is not needed here.
whyNot.3: The business layer decides on project-level exceptions; this is within the PM's authority.

B.q: Brennan Mutual's audit committee wants a written update every month. Project manager Mairi Campbell proposes monthly highlight reports during each stage, plus end stage reports and board decisions at each stage boundary. Which statement explains why she needs both kinds of control?
options: Event-driven controls replace the need for reports
Monitoring is time-driven; decisions are event-driven
Highlight reports are produced when an exception occurs
Time-driven controls are set by the business layer
B.why: Monitoring and reporting need a time-based approach, while control and decision-making are event-based, so both are needed in every stage (11.2.2).

whyNot.0: Event-driven controls complement regular reporting; they do not replace it.
whyNot.2: Highlight reports are time-driven; exception reports are the event-driven ones.
whyNot.3: The board agrees reporting frequency with the PM; the business layer sets project tolerances.

B.q: On Project Skyline, Stratoshift's delivery lead Arjun Menon forecasts that the wave 2 work package will exceed its time tolerance by four days. The wave migration stage as a whole is still forecast to finish within its tolerance. He tells the project manager. Who should decide how to deal with this?
options: The project manager, in controlling a stage
The project board, after an exception report
The executive committee, as the business layer
The senior supplier, Lena Fischer
B.why: Work-package-level exceptions are handled by the project manager in controlling a stage; only stage and project exceptions go to the board (11.2.6).

whyNot.1: The stage is within tolerance, so there is no stage exception to report to the board.
whyNot.2: The business layer decides on project-level exceptions.
whyNot.3: The senior supplier commits supplier resources but does not manage work package exceptions.

B.q: Tarnside College's project manager Leah Whitfield drafts the work package description for installing the welding bays. It includes tolerances for time, cost, scope and benefits. Which change should she make to the draft?
options: Remove the scope tolerance
Add a project cost tolerance
Move time tolerance to the team plan
Remove the benefits tolerance
B.why: Work package descriptions carry tolerances for scope, cost and time; benefits and quality tolerances are not agreed in a work package description (7.5, 11.2.1).

whyNot.0: Scope tolerance is one of the tolerances agreed in a work package description.
whyNot.1: Project tolerances are set by the business layer and do not belong in a work package description.
whyNot.2: Time tolerance for the work package is agreed between the PM and team manager in the description.

C.q: On Brennan Mutual's Project Skyline, the enterprise architect proposes that the new project dashboard should set each migration wave's tolerances automatically from past migration data, with no decision by the board or project manager. Is this an appropriate use of data in the progress practice, and why?
options: Yes, because data removes manual consolidation
Yes, because past performance predicts the future
No, because management levels set tolerances
No, because past data is no guide to future work
C.why: Data and systems support tracking and forecasting, but tolerances are set by the management levels: board for stages, PM for work packages (11.2.1, 11.2.7).

whyNot.0: Automation does save manual consolidation, but that does not explain who should set tolerances.
whyNot.1: Past data helps forecasting, but tolerances are still a management decision.
whyNot.3: Stored past performance can help predict future performance, so this reason is wrong.

C.q: Carrowford's half marathon project is in its build-up stage, which has a time tolerance of two weeks. Project manager Kezia Oduya's forecasts show that approval of the event safety plan will be three weeks late. To avoid alarming the board, she waits until the approval date has actually passed before raising an exception report. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because exceptions are reported once they occur
Yes, because the PM may act within stage tolerance
No, because a forecast breach needs escalating now
No, because the PM should ask the business layer
C.why: An exception is a situation where a breach of tolerance can be forecast; manage by exception aims to alert the next level as early as possible (11.1, 2.5).

whyNot.0: Exceptions are based on forecasts, not on actual breaches.
whyNot.1: The PM may act within stage tolerance, but this forecast exceeds it.
whyNot.3: Stage tolerance is the board's, so the exception report goes to the board.

C.q: Fernhollow Kitchen is in its development stage, which has a time tolerance of two weeks. The chefs forecast that one recipe will be signed off four days late, and the stage is still forecast to finish within tolerance. Project manager Nadia Osei sends an exception report to the board, because she thinks the board should hear of any slippage. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because the board should know about each delay
Yes, because exceptions alert the next level early
No, because it is within stage tolerance
No, because the team manager should raise it
C.why: If the PM can resolve an issue within stage tolerance, no exception report is needed; the board is kept informed through highlight reports (11.2.6).

whyNot.0: The board manages by exception and sees routine progress in highlight reports.
whyNot.1: Early alerts matter when tolerance is forecast to be breached, which it is not here.
whyNot.3: Team managers report to the PM; exception reports to the board come from the PM.

reteach.title: Driving to a wedding with a satnav
reteach.question: You must arrive within 15 minutes of the planned time. The satnav updates every few minutes. When should you phone ahead?

blocks.h: Check often, act on the forecast
blocks.body: The satnav's regular arrival-time updates are time-driven monitoring, like highlight reports. Reaching the motorway junction where you choose a route is an event-driven decision point, like a stage end. Your 15 minutes is the tolerance. If the satnav forecasts you will be 30 minutes late, you phone ahead now: that is the exception report. Waiting until you are actually late helps nobody. A five-minute delay within tolerance? Just take a quicker route yourself.

blocks.text: Phone ahead at update 4, when the forecast first crosses 15 minutes, not when you finally arrive late.

explain.h: Where the exception plan is made
explain.body: After the board receives an exception report and asks for an exception plan, the project manager prepares it in managing a stage boundary; the board then approves it in directing a project.

test.q: Wenmoor Community Health's board has reviewed an exception report about a three-week configuration delay and asked for an exception plan for the pilot stage. In which process should project manager Ellie Chandran prepare it?
options: Controlling a stage
Directing a project
Managing product delivery
Managing a stage boundary
test.why: Exception plans are prepared in managing a stage boundary, at the board's request, and approved by the board in directing a project (11.3.1).

whyNot.0: Controlling a stage is where the exception report is raised, not where the exception plan is prepared.
whyNot.1: Directing a project is where the board requests and approves the plan; the PM prepares it elsewhere.
whyNot.2: Managing product delivery is the team manager's process for work packages.

explain.body: Tolerances for the whole project come from the business layer. The board sets stage tolerances and the PM sets work package tolerances.

test.q: Wenmoor's executive team says it will accept a cost variation of plus or minus 10% and a delay of up to one month to the end of the roll-out; anything beyond that must go to the trust board. What are these limits?
options: Stage tolerances agreed by the project board
Work package tolerances set by the PM
Project tolerances from the business layer
Risk appetite set by the project board
test.why: Limits for the whole project set above the project board are project tolerances, set by the business layer (11.2.1).

whyNot.0: Stage tolerances are set by the board for each stage, not for the whole roll-out.
whyNot.1: Work package tolerances are set by the PM for individual work packages.
whyNot.3: Risk appetite is the business's attitude to risk; these are measurable cost and time limits.

explain.body: Progress reviews should forecast as well as look back, so problems are spotted early and the board can act.

test.q: On Tarnside College's project, the governors' finance committee has asked to be told at once of any forecast overspend. Project manager Leah Whitfield's highlight reports list costs to date but give no forecast of the final cost. How well does this apply the progress practice, and why?
options: Well, because highlights report actual progress
Well, because forecasts belong in end stage reports
Poorly, because highlights should go to governors
Poorly, because reviews should also look forward
test.why: Progress reviews should include forecasts of the objectives, not only actuals, so deviations can be seen early (11.1, 11.2.5).

whyNot.0: Actuals are needed, but without forecasts a coming overspend cannot be spotted early.
whyNot.1: Forecasts are part of regular progress reporting, not saved for the stage end.
whyNot.2: Highlight reports go to the project board; the issue is the missing forecast.

explain.body: Reporting frequency and format can be tailored to the project and audience, for example short online briefings for a dispersed, part-time board.

test.q: Wenmoor's project team and board work part-time across three localities. The board agrees that highlight reports will be given as a short online call at lunchtime, backed by a one-page dashboard, instead of a long written report. Is this appropriate, and why?
options: Yes, because reporting format can be tailored
Yes, because highlight reports are optional
No, because highlight reports must be documents
No, because the board should meet in person
test.why: Tailoring adjusts the frequency and formality of reports to the project; a virtual highlight for a dispersed board is appropriate (2.7, 11.2.4).

whyNot.1: Highlight reports are part of the board's time-driven control; the change is to their format.
whyNot.2: Management products can be produced in different formats when tailored.
whyNot.3: Boards can work virtually; meeting in person is not required.
